claims.text: Adding approximately 0.5 at.% Hf to a refractory NbMoTaWTi-type high-entropy alloy will enhance its high-temperature mechanical strength.
Trace Hf addition will promote fine Hf-rich intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries and interfaces.
The Hf-rich precipitates will strengthen the alloy by pinning dislocations.
Trace Hf will stabilize grain-boundary deformation mechanisms at high temperatures.
Approximately 0.5 at.% Hf will leave the alloy density nearly unchanged.
Approximately 0.5 at.% Hf will not adversely affect room-temperature deformation mechanisms or significantly degrade room-temperature performance.

Small Hf additions to single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys can improve room-temperature mechanical properties without significantly reducing ductility through precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases.
Prior Hf-addition studies cited here primarily concern single-phase high-entropy alloys and use Hf concentrations greater than 1 at.%.
The baseline NbMoTaWTi-type refractory alloy has moderate room-temperature ductility and high density.
A relevant baseline or similar refractory alloy has a high-temperature yield strength of approximately 405 MPa.
Relative to the Hf-free baseline, the Hf-containing alloy will show a 10–20% increase in high-temperature yield strength.
The predicted strength improvement should hold at approximately 1600 °C under tensile loading.
The Hf-containing alloy should maintain room-temperature ductility similar to the Hf-free baseline.
Higher Hf concentrations may cause excessive intermetallic formation and embrittlement.
The effect of trace Hf may depend on matrix composition and processing conditions.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing identically processed Hf-free and approximately 0.5 at.% Hf samples of the same refractory-alloy base composition.
A high-temperature yield-strength increase below 10% relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
Significant degradation of room-temperature mechanical performance would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe fine Hf-rich precipitates would falsify the proposed mechanism.
